utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today is Thursday, the 5th of February, 2009. I would like to greet all the people present in the courtroom, the representatives of the OTP, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people assisting us in the courtroom. I would like the registrar to make a correction on one of our exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is a correction to the document that was tendered yesterday and originally numbered P831, under seal. The correct number should read Exhibit P830, under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Now a housekeeping matter I'd like to deal with straight away. Mr. Seselj has two hours for his cross-examination. There might be a re-examination after that. Let's reckon on two to three hours. We were supposed to finish at 6.30 so we will have a break at five to 4.00 until 20 past 4.00 and then run through until 6.00 so that we gain some time. We will gain 20 minutes. This is what I wanted to announce. Mr. Seselj, you will have two hours for your cross-examination. We will bring the witness into the courtroom. Let me specify, I won't give the name of the witness due to come next week. I asked the witness to be there as of Wednesday onwards. I hope that's not a problem. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Should be no problem, Mr. President. That's the only witness we have for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we will hold our hearing on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to warn you that the Prosecution has just 7 hours left, 7 hours at its disposal and a few minutes plus. And I suggest that you put a suggestion to the Prosecution that during those 7 hours, they should bring forward only relevant witnesses which have to do with the indictment, testifying about the indictment, not as witnesses from locations that don't exist in the indictment at all because if after everything, the Trial Chamber is given addition -- the Trial Chamber gives the OTP additional time, that will be a scandal for the public, the broader public, after all this wasted time to add more time to the Prosecution. And the Prosecution has 7 hours and a few odd minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you have said is on the transcript. We are in open session. Mr. Seselj, I'll give you the floor now. Please make sure that you don't say anything which would lift the identity of the witness because I will then have to redact parts of the transcript. So I trust you will be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-1066 [as interpreted], what I'm most interested in, looking at the whole of your testimony, is the meeting in Mali Zvornik, and I'm sure you will understand why I'm most interested in that because that is a rally that is incorporated into the indictment. Everything else that you testified more or less has got nothing to do with the indictment against me but that rally and the one you described to me is directly quoted in the indictment, so I would like it to be clear to you while you -- why I insist on that. You mentioned the rally and you explained to us the attending features. Now I'm not clear on one point. You said that the rally was, first of all, scheduled to be held out in the open and that when we saw how many people had rallied there we asked to go inside. Did you say something like that, something similar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now I'd like to remind you that several days before the meeting, quite a few days before, there were posters stuck up all over Mali Zvornik and some posters across the Drina River in Veliki Zvornik; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't move around Mali Zvornik much so I didn't see them all. There were a few posters right across the bridge, but in Veliki Zvornik there were many posters, almost on every building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we scheduled the meeting in the large hall of the cultural centre, and I have two pieces of evidence to prove that that really was the case. First, that we scheduled the meeting to be held, the rally to be held outside where there was a stage set up and loud speakers and everything else that is done when you hold an outside rally. Now, you weren't able to see the stage and weren't able to see -- to hear any loudspeakers or anything; right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came a little late, as I said in my testimony yesterday just before the meeting began, the rally began so I saw no stage, no sound systems or anything but the Serbs whom I worked with, as far as I was able to gather from them and their colleagues, actually we learned that the rally would be held outside. Now, I didn't enter into the details as to whether that was true or not but I wanted to attend the rally and what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. My recollection is slightly different and I would like you to clarify this with the witness, if possible. I think I heard the witness indicate yesterday that the reason why the meeting was moved to take place inside was for security reasons because such a large crowd in which there would be a number of persons who would be hostile to the war issue could be dangerous for you. So that was why, if I understood the witness correctly, but I would invite you to clarify this. That was why it was decided ultimately to move the meeting inside, that would be safer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harhoff, we're going to deal with that rally for at least an hour and I do wish to convince you that we are going to clarify during that hour all the details concerning that rally because you know the sentence that is ascribed to me is entered directly into the indictment, because it's very interesting that we clear up all the details in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So let me ask you: Your information according to which the rally was supposed to be outside, out in the open, was something you heard from the people when you arrived but you didn't say it -- you didn't see it on the poster, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it up on the poster. I didn't have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since there was no stage and no sound system, and loud speakers, it was logical to suppose that the meeting wasn't scheduled, the rally wasn't scheduled to be held outside. And let me tell you that the cultural centre is right by the main road which passes through Mali Zvornik, along the Drina River valley.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And had we held a rally there, we would have blocked the whole main road, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's a large space. You can turn off the road to go to the cultural centre. There is a large parking lot so several thousand people could have been there, and what I saw was, say, a little over a thousand people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There might have been 2.000, I seem to remember a lot of people for such a small place. Of course it's difficult to say exactly how much.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, more than a thousand, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The second reason which goes to show -- well, if we had scheduled a meeting to be held out in the open and then go into a building, that would be impossible to arrange with the cultural centre because if you want to go inside, you would have to rent out the space in advance, you have to pay for the hall you're going to use and ensure all the other prerequisites for a rally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you thought attended the scheduling of meetings and rallies, but there were always alternatives for security reasons. There was always another option and that's why you changed your decision and decided to hold it inside in the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the rules and regulations in Serbia were the same as in Bosnia-Herzegovina which said that every political party had to inform the police that they intended to hold a rally, inform them in advance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never organised such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that that was the law. If you wanted to hold a rally, you had to inform the police thereof at least two days before the rally, say where the rally was going to take place, how long, whether security service was organised and so on and so forth, and had the OTP conducted a serious investigation, they would have provided us with the documents to show us where the rally was scheduled first. And I insist that it was scheduled to take place inside. Now, you gave us some facts. You said that many people turned up and that many people who were hostile to us turned up too, more hostile people than those who supported us. What would you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that there were more people who were hostile towards you. It was to be assumed that it might have been a 50:50 ratio. Why? Because Veliki Zvornik is mostly Muslim and mali Zvornik is a 50:50 ratio of percentage of the population, so we could assume that there were those from both sides; those who were for you, for the rally and the things you propagated and those who were opposed, against. It was difficult to assess all this to see who was in favour of whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Those who were against us were mostly Muslims, but there were Serbs, Communists who opposed us, too, together with the Muslims, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I know that? How would I know whether someone was a Communist and whether they were opposed or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you do know that there were many Serbs that took the Muslim side against us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many honourable and decent people were against the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We're not talking about who was honourable and decent and who was not. Those are value arguments and not facts. Let's stick to the facts for the time being. I'm not saying whether you're honest or not honest; I'm not interested in that. All I want is, with your help, to clarify the facts. Do we understand each other on that score? Now, we arrived there and some people greeted us with ovations and applause, a portion of the people there; whereas the others abused us, swore at us. Did you see that they carried Tito's photographs, too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered the hall before you. I didn't see you when you arrived. I just saw you when you were in the room because I learned that the rally would be held in the hall and not outside, so I couldn't see those pictures or the applause or the ovations or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well the pictures were brought in before we arrived.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the pictures had to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to remind you. If you remember those photographs, well and good; if not -- and don't try and speed me up. I have two hours. There is no need to speed up the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was just trying to help you out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, thank you, then. Thank you for helping me on that score, but some people who were opposed to us had photographs of Tito, framed photographs that they'd taken off walls and they were protesting. You didn't see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I went into the hall before you, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you discussed the situation with some of the people after the rally, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the rally resounded in the public, newspapers went on writing about it for days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Because of the incident that took place, so you had a chance of talking to people and hearing of their impressions from the rally and they could have told you that when we arrived there, that there were a lot of policemen. You saw the policemen too, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that police made a cordon so that we could enter the cultural centre building safely and securely, me together with my associates, seven or eight of us. And do you remember that there was a police line, a cordon, they cordoned off the area so that we could enter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You entered with another man and you sat down, you occupied a chair that was intended for you, and I saw two or three bodyguards who stayed up by the door but I didn't see anybody else. I saw you and this other man who sat down at the table that you were meant to use and your bodyguards state behind at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, the rally started and do you remember that, from time to time, you could hear people outside who were in opposition? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many people did you say were in the hall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a large hall. I would say that there were up to 80 people, not more than 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You see it's the largest cinema hall that Mali Zvornik has, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never in that cultural centre, but I don't remember. I would say 80 people and you could see this on the basis of your speech, when you said, I'm sorry that we couldn't hold the meeting outside so that everybody can hear what I have to say and hear you, and you said, I hope that you are worthy representatives of your organisations and that you will be able to convey to them what I'm going to say here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now you said that you were sitting in the last row with some other 15 or 20 Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If that last line has 20 seats, that last row has 20 seats, I don't suppose this cinema hall had just four rows. As far as I remember, it had at least 20 rows, although I can't remember exactly; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can count them because I remember it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how many rows, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember every detail and I would say in my assessment there were not more than 80 people in the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, precisely because you are reducing that number, you're telling me a smaller number, that is something I find intimately unacceptable. I'm trying to show you how many seats the hall had and all the seats were full; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether all the seats were occupied, but that's how many people I thought there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, we went outside and once again, there was this cordoned offer area by the police in front of the entrance and we were moving towards our cars which were parked a little further away, and stones and other objects were being thrown at us; is that right? Do you remember that? Do you remember that that was how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement yesterday, I said that in the parking lot, there was a group of people and one of them opened the boot of the car --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's take it one by one. Let's take it in order. This car and the boot of the car came later.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely as you were coming out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We were coming out of the hall, we were being -- stones were being thrown from the crowd, there was a lot of people moving around, some members of the police tried to spit at us. Was it like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't close to you but I saw that you were knocked down to the ground and that your bodyguards were on top of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And we were the target of stones. We came out to this broader plateau and stones began to hit the people who were on top of me; isn't that correct? Now you claim that I was hit. I actually was not hit. You also claimed that the next day, you saw me on television with bandages on my head. This is simply not true. I was not hit by a single stone but the stone did -- stones did hit people who were around me, Miladin Todosijevic was one of them who was hit by a stone. There was Vineta Marinovic, journalist from Velika Serbia, she was hit by a stone in the chest, and some other people also were hit by stones. Then the people from our municipal committee from Mali Zvornik took out these wooden bats from the trunk of the car, perhaps a metre long or something.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little bit shorter than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you could see that these were freshly cut pieces of wood, and then people started to run away, some people were running towards the bridge and others were running along the road next to the cafe that was opposite from the culture hall. I recall this large number of people who were running in that direction. Did you se that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't paying attention. I wasn't able to see where people were running. I was trying to save myself so that I don't get pulled into this whole game so that I pulled back, I hid myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. So then there was a big fight that occurred, a lot of people were hurt, and then after that, I with my associates left for Banja Koviljaca, we had dinner there and we spent the night at the Banja Koviljaca hotel. I wasn't hurt and you could not have seen my head in bandages. Not then, no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall saying yesterday that I saw you on television but I saw you in the media, in the newspapers, your photograph with a band-aid on the left, or I don't know what side of your face, and your hand was bandaged also so this could have been something that happened overnight. Were you hurt in Banja Koviljaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, it didn't happen there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So how come had you a band aid there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I never had a band aid on my head. I don't know where you saw that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well let's look at that perhaps in the newspapers. After 17 years it won't be so hard to find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A lot of newspapers wrote about that and there was a wide, broad debate about that. Do you know that the Serbian Radical Party has its own newspaper, the newspaper called Velika Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't able to read that paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does it still have that newspaper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, regardless of the fact that those newspapers made you sick, we will have to read a little bit from that newspaper.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we put on the ELMO, please, this article from Velika Serbia which talks about the promotion of our party in Mali Zvornik. I asked the registrar to provide copies, the Prosecution has a copy. Do you have the whole newspaper? All right. We will look at the newspaper later. Now what we are going to look at is just this particular article. Have you put it on ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, can you look at the title of this article. Do you see what it says here? Serbian Chetnik Movement promoted the party in Mali Zvornik. So we promoted the Serbian Chetnik Movement, this is what we called it. It could have been the Serbian Radical Party promotion but this was a Chetnik promotion, wasn't it? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You can see from the contents in the culture hall, you can see the Chetnik flags, pictures of Draza Mihajlovic, and so on and so forth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We had all of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please can you be a little bit patient. This is such an interesting discussion. Please have a little bit of patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's indeed a very interesting discussion. I'm wondering if the accused would let us know whether he is conceding that the article is about the rally that took place in Mali Zvornik in March of 1992 or whether he's putting something else before the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, I'm not going to be explaining to you in advance what my goal is. Please have some patience. You are directly interfering in the concept of my cross-examination. Please don't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the witness is being led to believe that this article is about the rally that he has described in his testimony, that's the way it's being presented to the witness, I think it's significant that we are aware of what the accused's position is on that because otherwise he is setting the witness up. So we need to know what the date of this article is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is that rally. There is no other rally where a fight broke out, only -- a fight broke out at only one meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the first line of this article it says, "On the 4th of August this year, a delegation of the Serbian Chetnik Movement came to Mali Zvornik." Why is the 4th of August being mentioned here if this was in March? What is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it could be a typo. Now let us look at those photographs. Do you see here two people in the hall holding up a photograph of Draza Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you see the first row, the front row of the hall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a little bit blurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you cannot see Branko Grujic in the first row, and do you see this photograph where you can the crowd outside and the police, there is a policeman prominent in the front of picture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't really see that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you can see the police cap in the photograph, it's towards the bottom of the photograph. The introductory part of the article talks about our arrival and I'm giving an interview there for the Radio Podrinje and Radio Sabac. And then you can turn to the following page. On the following page, we can see how the stage is decorated, where we were sitting, the podium and you can see the president of our Mali Zvornik municipal board who opened this rally and you can see Vojin Vuletic who at the time was our general secretary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you don't know these people. Anyway, turn to the next page. On the next page, you can see Vojin Vuletic and then below that you can see the working Presidency where I am sitting. The first to the left is lawyer Milorad Vukosavljevic. At the time he was our vice-president; he died a few years after that. And then we see our officials from Mali Zvornik. In the middle there is myself, then next to me Aleksander Stefanovic, the general secretary; and lawyer Olivera Jelkic. I can recognise them all. This is a central photograph. In a small photograph you can see Oliver Jelkic entering the hall and then below you can see lawyer Milorad Vukosavljevic entering. All right. And then on this page, we can see that it says that the article is written by Vineta Marinovic, who was actually hit by a stone at that rally. This is the central part of it. Maybe we can zoom it up a little bit. Then members of the central Serbian Chetnik Movement entered the hall and then our president of the executive hall welcomed the speakers, Glamocanin was there, who was the member of the inner leadership, and then the first speaker was Aleksandar Stefanovic. Please turn to the next page. You can see a part of the hall here and then a part of the working Presidency. You can see myself and then Aleksandar Stefanovic. You can see this text on the side where he talks about Draza Mihajlovic. Do you remember that the first speaker was Aleksandar Stefanovic and that he talked about Draza Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that man. Please don't ask me about the names, I don't know any of these people by name. I was talking about your speech, about your address, what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Let's skip his speech because he talks about the life of Draza Mihajlovic as whole here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few seconds, if this meeting was held on August 4th, we can understand that because we see that Mr. Seselj is in a shirt, short-sleeved shirt, it was probably hot, so it might be on August 4th. But if I understood right, in this room we saw photographs and you should be at the very end of the room, at the -- in the far -- at the very far end of the room so we should see you, normally.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't see the whole of the hall, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Here we see the far end of the room. There's probably less than 80 people but we see people sitting in all those rows; and if you are there, you should be in the bottom row, in the last row; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Is the question addressed to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If you actually attended this meeting on August 4th, you would be at the far end of this room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last row where I was sitting, I was sitting there with people whom I mentioned, Muslims, in the last row next to the wall, and you cannot clearly see my face. You cannot see my face in the back row. The photograph -- I mean, was taken, if it was taken from this rally, but since this is a text that was written and talks about a rally of the 4th of August, and Seselj is standing at the podium in short sleeves, but in March in Bosnia, it's quite cold. You cannot walk around in T-shirts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, these people who were sitting here, they're wearing T-shirts, short-sleeved T-shirts. This doesn't -- this could not be a photograph from the time that we are discussing. I am definitely sure about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Continue. Yes, proceed, Mr. Seselj. We'll see as we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the following page, please. Now, well, here you can see the front row here. On the following page, Aleksandar Stefanovic finished his speech and now Srdjan Glamocanin is speaking and he is a member of the government. And in the photograph, in the middle, you can see the front row. In the front row we can see the journalist of Velika Serbia, Vineta Marinovic, and we can see some other people and you cannot see Branko Kljuic anywhere. Srdjan Glamocanin again is speaking about Serbdom, about the Serbian history, the traditions of its heros, and then you can see a photograph of the crowd in front of the hall, this is the bottom photograph. Can you please scroll up? You can see this crowd in front and now please turn to the following page. You can see the police cordon in front and they are trying to secure a safe passage for us, these are the first two photographs, and then the third photograph was taken at some point during the meeting. In front of the hall you can see police and some citizens. Please turn to the following page. On the following page you can see lawyer Milorad Vukosavljevic who is the vice president of the central homeland administration. He gave quite a long speech. Can you please turn to the next page. You've skipped a page. Look at page 30, please. This is page 30. There is no photograph on this page. And then here it would be interesting to read what he says about Muslims. So could you please read what I have marked here?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note: We need to know exactly where the accused is reading from in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps your copy is not marked. I marked it on my copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On that page, you can see at the bottom, Tito Ustasha, get the House of Flowers out. And then it says, Natasha Vukosavljevic. I am having a problem with these blurred letters.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Underneath this text, Tito Ustasha, House of Flowers, I don't know why you are asking me. The second reason that may be particularly happy when I was called to -- when I was invited to speak to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Well, perhaps it will be easier for me to read. Let me do it. That you people are the living proof of the brazen life that the Yugoslav army committed genocide against Muslims in the fatherland. I think that in your midst, more than half of Muslims might be of Serbian origin. Some remember the stories of their ancestors, that once they were part of the Serbian people. Draza Mihajlovic was the Defence Minister of the emigre government or the government in exile in London. You know that, you're quite an educated man.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but I don't know why you are interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you don't need to know that. You're here to testify about facts. Who cares why I want to know. Perhaps I went mad during the night. And a lot of people think that I am mad anyway and you agree with them, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, a lot of people do think that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well let's continue in a more jovial atmosphere. Some -- I will continue. Some remember the stories of their ancestors, that once they were part of the Serbian people. Some do not remember this while other even think they are Turks. However, at the moment, we do not need to focus on this at this time. It is very difficult to define the ethnic origin of your fellow citizens. These are Serbs who lost their awareness and memory. It was easy to mercilessly push them, especially the so-called "fukara," scum, into a fratricidal war in 1941 as surrogates, where they slaughtered their innocent neighbours and yesterday's friends when they were offered Serbian property. Therefore, your duty here above all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj. Mr. Seselj, I'm totally confused now regarding your cross-examination. Before starting to read this document, could you please stop and try and determine whether this is the rally which the witness testified or whether it's another rally. Just a minute. Hold on. Otherwise we're wasting time. Normally, when the Prosecution is presenting documents, you always want him to tell you exactly what the context is, what the date is for this document, and so forth and so on, and we always say you're right and grant you this opportunity. So you should do the same thing for the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For everyone, I will read this quickly. In the Prosecution's pre-trial brief on Zvornik, this is what the Prosecution says: In March 1992, the Serbian Bosnian forces had created their own police in Zvornik and had declared that this city was a Serbian municipality and was about to -- was about to attack to -- supported by the JNA. In the same month, in March, Vojislav Seselj gave a speech in Mali Zvornik, a municipality in front of Zvornik, on the other side of the Drina, and he said on that occasion, and I quote what he allegedly would have said: "My Chetnik brothers, and I am mainly to talking to those of you who are on the other side of the Drina, you, the bravest of the bravest, we are about to cleanse Bosnia of the unfaithful and to show them the way that will take them back to the east, the east where they belong." Mr. Seselj's words which are quoted or footnoted, footnote 291 and on footnote 291, it says, "VS-2000." Therefore, these words, these underlying words are quoted from what the witness heard and what he heard in March. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If I may further address this issue, Your Honours. The accused is, in my respectful submission, misleading the witness. I have here the full copy of Velika Serbia in which this article is drawn from and it is an issue of Velika Serbia that is dated the 15th of August, 1990. And this was why I asked the accused earlier on whether he agreed that this meeting was actually about the same meeting that the witness has testified about. The article has nothing to do with the meeting that the witness has testified about, and these attempts of showing photographs and getting the witness confused about the presence of various people is completely appropriate. And the accused is laughing now, he's fully aware of what's going on. If Your Honours would like to see the copy, I can hand it up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the indictment, in the indictment, the speech was made in March.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, how does the Prosecution know what it talks about? I assume I've shown you and proved that all the Prosecution witnesses were false witnesses. You didn't have a single one brought in here by the Prosecution who was not a false witness and tried to support the thesis in the indictment, not a single one. This is a rally that took place at the beginning of August -- go on, just you interrupt me. Interrupt me, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, this has nothing to do with the question you were being asked. We want to you determine what this refers to and then we'll see, but right now you cannot start lecturing or making speeches on all the witnesses we've heard up until now. You are just making fun of the Trial Chamber right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the document we have here is dated August 15, 1990. So this might be a document that is edited with prior articles, maybe, maybe, so what we have seen, maybe that's August 4th, 1992, I don't know, but please try and figure out what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that I have turned out to be the silliest here. Mr. President, isn't it obvious the witness takes the meeting from August 1990 and testifies about it, representing it to be a meeting from March 1992. That's what he's doing. Am I an idiot or is it the Prosecution? One of the sides must be. He's describing a rally that took place in 1990, and I'm going to prove that to you now by looking at the last page of that article, and may we look at page 36 now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we're not accusing anyone, we're not accusing you, we're not accusing the witness. But we have a problem. The witness told the Prosecutor that this meeting, rally had been held in March 1992, and you are saying that this was in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, well, the witness could have told the Prosecution that I personally killed a million people. What do I care what the witness told the Prosecution. I am going to overthrow his testimony here and every time you interrupt me in cross-examination, you want to undermine my cross-examination. The more perfect it is, the more you want to undermine it and you want to prevent me from saying that these are false witnesses. From all the indices, all the indicators show -- well, why don't you listen to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, don't say that we're trying to undermine your cross-examination. We're doing everything to try to shed light on this. I took time to read the pre-trial brief in order to know what the Prosecution's case was. And the Prosecution's case here is based on what this witness said. And now, I'm all ears to listen to your cross-examination and your demonstration and your case, so please put your case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the only witness through which the Prosecution wishes to base its thesis that in March 1992, I held a rally in Mali Zvornik and said what is quoted in the indictment, "Dear brother Serbs, we should expel those who do not believe in God and so on." There's not another one. And I want to show you that the meeting in Mali Zvornik did not take place in March 1992 but in August 1990 and that this witness is describing that meeting and then adding false words to what he's saying. Listen, we have the coordinates for this meeting. There was a brawl, a physical settling of accounts. The police intervened, members of my party took out poles from their cars to chase away the rabble that attacked us, so we have all the right coordinates. The whole of Serbia, the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina knows full well that the only rally at which this mass brawl broke out was in Mali Zvornik in 1990. In March 1992, look at all the Serbian press, there was no meeting in Mali Zvornik. What do I care what the Prosecution is writing, as if that were the only silly things they wrote. We're talking about a 1990 rally and here is proof. The last page of the article, and we're going to read it all, at least the whole of my speech or I'm not going to carry on my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, one small detail that you provided us with that might be interesting. This rally would allegedly have been held in August 1990.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And here's proof. The last page of the article, page 36. Can we have that page, please. The rally ends. Can we scroll down, please. Scroll up. The upper part. Above the photograph. And zoom in on that, please. This is what Vineta Marinovic, the journalist, writes in Velika Serbia in a 3rd issue in August 1990. This is what she writes: "Everybody gets up and leaves the room quietly and calmly. We have no idea what is waiting for us outside. In the meantime, the police has arrived and formed a human shield with the aim of allegedly protecting us from the mass of Muslim fundamentalists gone mad who were shouting outside. We soon realised that it would be much better if the police hadn't come at all, and this alleged protection of theirs jeopardised us even further. "The militant fundamentalists fought in their typical way. Literally protected by the police, they threw big stones at us, they spat at us and they yelled at the top of their voices. They were swearing at us and using words like infidels and welakins [phoen], welakin mothers," and that is the term they use for the Orthodox. I'm reading it rather quickly because you have the English translation. "They looked like savage beasts -- ravaged beasts. However, we did not run away from them and we did not respond to their barking. We did not want to give them that pleasure. We did not wish to leave our brothers, the Orthodox Serbs from Mali Zvornik. We did not want to run away from our Serbian land. We all stood together with the Vojvoda at the head. We stood there unprotected, calmly talking the insults, stones and humiliations as only the Orthodox Serbs know how. "Encouraged by the help and protection of the police, the gathered Muslims became even more furious and began throwing stones at the nearby parked cars of the Serbs who were parked there. Almost all the windows of the cars were broken, and Miladin Todosijevic, a member of the central fatherland department, was hit in the head by a stone which made a huge cut on his forehead and blood gushed forth. When the men from the Serbian Chetnik Movement of Mali Zvornik saw this, they grabbed some wooden poles and in self-defence, charged at the crowd which, small wonder -- little wonder, started fleeing as fast as their legs could carry them. They showed once again that they were capable of fighting only with a dagger, hammer or small knife in their hand, with tied or captured Serbs, women, children, the elderly. It was pathetic to see them fleeing, but that is in their blood and that will, as it seems, never change. "When everything calmed down, we all got into the cars and the column headed towards Banja Koviljaca where the hosts prepared a small feast for us, and during that feast, Vojvoda Seselj found time to talk to each and every one of those brave young Serbs, to listen to their problems, their difficulties, and troubles, the kind that they encountered daily and to advise them. Relief was visible on their faces, on their troubled faces, and a mild-note of gratitude was fell in their words. In spite of everything, they will now be able to sleep more calmly in the knowledge that they are not alone. The Serbian people and the Serbian Chetniks are with them." That was something that Vineta Marinovic wrote to describe the rally that the witness was talking about. It's the same rally, and she was bitten because she was hit by a stone too and had to seek medical assistance. And that is the bitter tone of the text out of that incident; but that is the sole rally, the only rally where this incident happened, no other rally -- there was no other rally like that. And this was published by the papers, the Muslim papers, and Radio Zvornik had broadcast the whole of the following day about that. And in March 1992, there was nothing in any of the papers, no trace of us having held a rally in Mali Zvornik at all. Why didn't the Prosecution investigate this? Because there's no intelligent man in the Prosecution to find this out on time and prevent them from making such stupid mistakes. That's not my fault. I'm here to demolish the indictment, and I have succeeded in demolishing it. So far there is not a single witness so far who had a successful piece of testimony that the Prosecution can use, and the fact that you hold closed sessions, that is just a sort of -- make people think that something was happening here. The public has to know that at the closed sessions, the false witnesses fair far worse than they do in open session, and my cross-examinations are even more successful during those sessions. That is something that they should know about. And this is proof and evidence that this was a rally held in August 1990. I wanted to do that in a calmer atmosphere, but you didn't let me do that. There was no other rally where an incident like this broke out. That was the only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, according to this newspaper, and the photographs that we see where there was incidents which corresponds to what you said, but here the date is August 1990. Why is it that you said that the rally was held in March 1992. Maybe you mixed things up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not confuse or mix up anything, absolutely nothing. And after all this I can provide at least 10 people, the names of 10 people that you can call, talk to them and hear their statements. The rally was held exactly in mid-March 1992, possibly there was another meeting in August, as it says in the papers, because I did notice the date. It says the 4th of August, 1992, possibly, but at that time, there was war in Zvornik municipality and there was shooting from Serbia into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm starting from the assumption that you're telling the truth and that in March 1992, there was a rally that was held; and in March 1992, stones were thrown, Mr. Seselj was hit and injured, et cetera, et cetera. But if that's the case, and if that is true, then it would just be a rerun of what actually had already happened in August 1992 because in August 1992, we had exactly the same problem. And the media who was very closely following Mr. Seselj would have written and -- so if what you are saying is true, if in March 1992, a rally was actually held, the media that was closely following Mr. Seselj should have written about this saying, Just like this August 1990, once again the members of the Serbian Radical Party were aggressed and so forth and so on, and we have nothing. So I'm really wondering whether you haven't mixed up the dates? I mean it's easy to understand, you know, with everything that happened and all the years that have gone by you might have mixed up the dates. Are you absolutely 100 percent sure of the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to observe something, to note something? On the 4th of August, 1992, there were no Muslims in Zvornik anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But who's talking about August 1992? We're talking about August 1990. The 4th of August, 1990, two years before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were then, but if we are talking about August 1992, then there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well nobody's mentioning August 1992. This is the 4th of August, 1990, that we're talking about, two years before the war. That's the rally we were referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm on my feet because the accused has essentially been testifying -- making submissions and so on, and he has asserted with some -- that -- excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, please don't indulge in procedure because here we are on a very important issue. We need to know whether Mr. Seselj said this in March, which is what the witness is saying or whether the speech was delivered in August 1990. This is crucial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, and I'm on my feet because when the accused testified in the Milosevic case, he was asked about this meeting on the 5th of September, 2005. And Mr. Milosevic asked him whether there had been a meeting in Mali Zvornik in March where he had made this particular statement, and he confirmed this, and he corrected the interpreter. And I have copies of the transcript here if you like, or it is at page 43.724 and the two following pages. So he has testified under oath about this in another case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, Mr. Milosevic asked you this question, and you said that the meeting had been held in March.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, let me see the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript I have in my hands, the question is as follows: "Is it true that in March, I believe that in your indictment it says March 1992, you delivered a speech in Mali Zvornik? Is this true? Did this happen?" Et cetera. Et cetera. And there, "Dear Chetnik brother, notably you who are across," blah, blah, and so forth and so on. It is your answer. This is partial forgery.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President, in my answer -- well, I don't know English at all, but I can that in my answer, I deal with the contents and not the date. I completely leave the date aside. I am proving to Mr. Milosevic that it was impossible for me to say something about pagans and so on - I'm calling the Muslims - I'm not an uneducated man, I'm explaining that the greatest Serbian bishop of the 20th century, Nikolaj Velimirovic represented Islam as the first radical variant of Protestantism in Christianity, and I go on to explain that. I don't deal with dates here. Milosevic is reading what it says in his indictment, I assume, and I can completely leave aside the date. I don't refer to that at all. I'm just showing that it was impossible for me to say something like that with my -- the education I have, but I don't confirm the date anywhere and you can see that the Prosecution is telling lies here in front of the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me refer to what you've said, Mr. Seselj, during the Milosevic trial did not say that he agreed with the months of March because when the question was put to him, he doesn't answer as regards the months of March, he says that this is a distortion of what he has said; and then he moves on to other topics. He doesn't admit this. He doesn't admit that it was in March. So you may have made a mistake, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We submit, in light of the significance of this particular issue which is the subject of the indictment of the accused, it is quite significant that all he corrects is -- he just addresses, Well I didn't say pagan, there's a mistake in the translation, the error is actually I said something that means waste or feces when he talks about the Muslims. That is a correction that he made. He has no other problem with the proposition that is being put to him. I'm not putting it forward for any other purpose but in our submission is the only thing he has to correct is this rather [Overlapping speakers] ...of the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. President, when I testified in the Milosevic case, I was responding to Mr. Milosevic's questions. I did not have any papers or documents in front of me in order to be able to corroborate everything. What was the most important thing to me at that time, to deny that it is absolutely impossible to give such a definition of Muslims as pagans and Godless people from my mouth and from my head. I was not concerned with the date. I did not link the dates with anything at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj and Mr. Marcussen to find out whether or not there was a rally on the 7th of March, 1992, I think should be a simple thing, and I would invite the Prosecution to provide further proof of this because it is in the indictment and in the pre-trial brief; and so when you have that proof, and if you can find it, you can bring it back and from thereon, I think we should just move on now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let them find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question for the witness, as I said a while ago. Usher, could you please place on the ELMO the third page of this newspaper article. 93, 93. Yes, Witness, we have here at the bottom far right, could you scroll the page up a little bit. Yes. What we have here are people who are sitting on the podium. Did these people attend the rally which you have referred to, i.e., the 4th of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see the faces very well here, and I didn't really try that much to notice who the people were, what they looked like. I didn't know them. I came out of curiosity, as I said yesterday, to see who this Seselj was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not asking you to recognise these people, to give us their identity, just could you tell us whether these four people sitting next to Mr. Seselj, whether, among these four people, there was a woman. You might be able to remember that. I don't know. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the table where he was sitting at that meeting, no women were sitting at the table. There were no women sitting at the same table as Seselj at that meeting. There was a man with a beard like this man in the dark jacket in the photograph, I remember that, but I definitely remembered that there were no women sitting next to him at that meeting when I was there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, Judges, it would be the best thing if the Prosecution searched all the Serbian and Bosnian press from March 1990 to see if there were any rallies of the Serbian Radical Party in Mali Zvornik. No such rally can go without being recorded by the press. If this incident did take place in March 1992, then it must have been written about and commented upon. The witness himself said that there were many comments in the press after that, but this was exclusively in August 1990 and nowhere else, and after that, they refused at the Ministry of Justice in Serbia to register our party. We thought that we had met all the requirements and that we would be able to register the party, but this did not happen; and we even suspected that perhaps these people were brought in by the regime to create some kind of disorder as a pretext based on which they would not register our party. There were no incident like this one that happened in Mali Zvornik at any other of the Serbian Radical Party, nothing like this ever happened before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, as my colleague Judge Harhoff has said, and I agree with him on this, if the Prosecution feels or holds that the rally was held on the 4th of March, 1992, you have to adduce evidence in support of this. For the time being, we don't have this evidence. There can be a lot of evidence. There can be press articles as Mr. Seselj has said. There can be police reports because when there is an incident, there is automatically a police report. So you could lay your hands on that. Otherwise, we have one rally which was held in March 1990 in -- in August, I apologise, in August 1990, and there were incidents during that rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will, of course, look further into this. There is evidence on record obviously from this particular witness, and I believe we have some other -- an intelligence report and some other evidence that supports this, but we'll probably get back to this later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Marcussen again is making things up, and this is not fitting for a Prosecutor of an international Tribunal. Look at the file that we were given by the Prosecutor. And the Prosecutor, to my surprise, did not use this in his examination in chief. This is Exhibit 1021. The Prosecutor has a police document of the 20th of April, 1992. I hope you found that. In the first paragraph, they talk about important events because the whole thing refers to a longer period of time and then the first paragraph -- sub-paragraph, the last sentence, says: "In Mali Zvornik on the 17th of March, 1992, was visited by the people's deputy Vojislav Seselj, who after a short talk went to Ljubovja." I wasn't just anybody then. I was a people's deputy. You don't believe then at that time, some kind of unruly crowd could lynch a people's deputy. The police says, who monitored my movements, he passed through Mali Zvornik. I briefly had a meeting with somebody there and then I went on to Ljubovja, and then after that to Bajina Basta, where I had a scheduled appearance on a radio programme. Here in this report, definitely it would be noted that there was some kind of incident. Had there been an incident where I was at the meeting, this definitely would have appeared in this report. The Prosecution would have received from the Serbian police all the documents where my name is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, what is the number of that document, did you say 1021.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1021, I think. That is another piece of evidence that there was no rally or meeting in Mali Zvornik. Well this is not good. How can this be good for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have document 1021. Mr. Marcussen, in this document 1021, we see that this is a report stemming from the Ministry of Defence regarding --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Interior, it's the police ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On my first page, it says Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the Defence, I apologise, it's my mistake, Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Ministry of Defence. Mr. Marcussen, at the time Mr. Seselj was an MP. When an MP travels, the intelligence services reports on this. If he came on the 4th of March to Mali Zvornik, there must have been a police report. It couldn't have been otherwise. Otherwise, the witness may be confused. Perhaps he thinks many years later that it happened in March, whereas it happened in August. Witness, when you said that this had happened in March 1992, in what year did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1996, on the 26th and the 27th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1996. On a personal note, I have attended a number of meetings at this Tribunal, and if you asked me which meeting I attended four years ago, I would be unable to tell you unless something extraordinary happened; for instance, if the President of the Tribunal has a heart attack, otherwise I would find it very difficult to remember that. So it was in 1996 that you said that you mentioned what had happened on -- in March 1992. This was in 1996, and you are quite sure about it. Mr. Seselj, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Considering that we have been discussing the contents of Prosecution Exhibit 65 ter number 1021, I would suggest that we admit it into evidence so that we have the document when the record is to be assessed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problems let's give it an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your honours, that will be Exhibit P831.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Mr.Seselj, continue with your questions, if any.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this an exhibit of the Defence or the Prosecution because the Prosecutor didn't want to use it yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the Prosecution, it's you who raised the issue so ... please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's important to me now, gentlemen, Judges, to study my entire speech from this meeting, so that we can see whether this speech contains the sentence that the witness asserts it contains. Now we have clarified when the meeting took place. There was no other meeting except this one. There was only a fight at this one, there were only poles in the trunk of the car at this meeting and our members chased away the crowd that was throwing stones at us. Again, can you scroll this up on the ELMO. We're not going -- [No interpretation] -- the following page, this is page 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The first photograph shows us coming out of the culture hall and then us walking down the street and stones flying all about us and then we have Vineta Marinovic, a journalist of Velika Serbia holding her chest where she was struck by a stone and Miladin Todosijevic is holding his head, which was bleeding. Immediately after the meeting we took them to Banja Koviljaca, to the emergency medical service. Can we scroll up, we can see Vineta Marinovic, journalist of Velika Serbia, holding her chest where she was hit on the head and next to her is Miladin Todosijevic, whose head is bleeding. He's holding some sort of handkerchief or something on his forehead. After that, we took the two of them to Banja Koviljaca to the emergency room. Can we now look at the next page, Vineta Marinovic ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, before you continue. Witness, assuming that in August 1990 these events occurred with this woman holding her head because she's been hit by a stone, and in light of the events that occurred, do you think that two years later the same political party will hold a rally in exactly the same place without taking the necessary measure to ensure that public law and order is abided by? Do you think one could contemplate that, that people who have been attacked come and hold the same rally to be attacked again? Do you think this makes sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it seems to me that there have to be precautions, and if this meeting was held in 1990, there must have been precautions taken; and for that reason, it must have been held inside the hall because of this number of people, the possibility of an incident occurring. So because of these precautionary measures, the meeting was held in the hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... is that if in 1990, if in August these incidents occurred and these incidents were serious despite the fact that there were a number of policemen around and stones were thrown and people were wounded, do you think that the people who organised this rally would organise it again a year and a half later. And a year and a half later, when you are a Muslim person, you walk into the room, you walk into the room in March of 1992, if what you are saying is true. Do you think this makes any sense at all? To my mind, there is something which we need to reflect upon. You have told us that you were in the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in the hall, that is true. And it's true that nobody checked our IDs, and there were 15 to 20 people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, up to 20 days before the armed conflict in Zvornik, there was so many weapons among the people, had something happened like then, there would have been hundreds of dead. You don't think that at a time like that, people would have been using stones and wooden poles. At that time, guns were already in play. Zvornik was full of weapons and volunteers. You don't believe for a minute that Muslims from Zvornik would come to Mali Zvornik to attack us with stones at that time. They -- there would have been a lot of casualties if they had done that at that time. I mean this is just a logical conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well I hope you managed to hear me. What I was saying is had this incident taken place in March 1992, two days before the armed conflict, there was so much weapons and so many soldiers and volunteers, at least 100 people would have been killed. There would not be an incident involving stones and wooden poles, March 1992 was an electrified atmosphere. It never entered our head to conduct the promotion of our party because an armed conflict was looming, and there was already various incident so that is why that is impossible. But there we go, the Prosecutor seems to think everything is possible. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: After Olivera Jelkic on the next page, page 32 and now a little patience, bear with me, because we're going to have to look at the whole of my speech to see if it contains that sentence. Last paragraph, can we see that, middle of the last paragraph? The president of the Serbian Chetnik Movement, Dr. Vojislav Seselj is speaking, and I say: Brothers and sisters, Serbian men and women, God be with us, God be with you. That's what you heard. Now would you help me out here, and let's take it paragraph by paragraph. Let's move it down one paragraph, please. A little more so we can see the top of the page. And then the last paragraph. The top of the page, please. The top. Well, it's the last column, my mistake. The third column. And the top of the page. It would be better if it were somebody who knew Serbian. Anyway. There we have it. Brothers and sisters, Serbian men and women, God be with you, and then the response is God be with you. That's a traditional Serb meeting, right? You heard at the beginning of the rally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, would you read out that first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brothers and sisters, Serbian men and women, God be with us, God be with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Next.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are gathered here today in Serbian Mali Zvornik at the promotion of the Serbian Chetnik movement party, it took almost half a century to restore the Serbian Chetnik sentiments and feeling in our people. The Serbian people lived for half a century in slavery akin to that of the Turks, and the Serbian people suffered during that slavery. During the last 50 years, the Serbian people did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Shall I take over. I think I can see better: The Serbian people did not resemble the Serb heros, the kind we know from Serbian ethnic poems. They did not look like the Serbs that fought wars with the Turks and won two Balkan wars, in the First World War. The Serbian people mostly looked like the people of sycophants and toadies. So I'm characterising the Serb people there under the Communist dictators, if that's quite obvious. There's nothing about the Muslims there, do you agree? Can I move on? Then I go on to say why was that so. Because all that was great in the Serbian people was killed in two Balkan wars and two World Wars, or took refugee in the emigration after the Second World War or was killed in Tito's camps and prisons. Now move the text down a bit. The Serbian people were biologically blemished and it took several decades for new generations to grow, to start straightening up and to bring back the old glory of the Serbian people, Serbian national pride and dignity. And right now we are living in that period of history and it is during this period of our history that the Serbian youth, in particular, are finding their own two feet, standing up against Communist dictatorship and all traditional Serbian enemies. So this is an anti-Communist and anti-regime speech, do you agree, Mr. 2000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to make any assessments and comments as to the nature of the speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you see that there is no mention of Muslims there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, do you think, Mr. Seselj, that somebody would be so clever as to write the blackest of what you said, and I said yesterday that you said that the Drina was not a boundary between Serbia and Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's what I think today. I don't think the Drina River can be a border.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But in that text, is there what I said when you got up and said categorically, brothers Chetniks and especially those of you across the Drina River, you are the bravest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's take it in order. We'll come to that. But I still maintain that the Drina is only a temporary border and cannot be a proper border dividing the Serbian people into two parts. "Today when we are finally bringing the anti-Serbian Communist dictatorship to an end we can see that as a people we really have to start from scratch. Communism destroyed almost all the Serbian traditional values. We have to restore our Serbian state. We, the Serbian Chetniks, want neither the Communist system nor Yugoslavia anymore. We realise that Yugoslavia was a stepmother to the Serbian people and that the Serbian people, especially in Communist Yugoslavia, lost almost everything they had." Is this an ultra-Serb nationalist speech; is that right? Right? Can you hear me? Is it a speech by a great Serbian nationalist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is. So we'll move on. I'm just asking you. "The villain and criminal Josip Broz Tito did all he could to disfigure Serbia by following orders of the Communist International and Vatican, and he almost succeeded in that. Three artificial ethnicities were created out of the Serbian national being: Montenegro, Macedonia and Muslim." Do you remember me saying that? Did I say that the Muslim nation was an artificial nation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You say that at all your meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did I say that then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. "Serbian lands were divided and torn apart. A large number of separate federal units were created out of the Serbian countries and lands. He made the Serbs quarrel amongst themselves. He introduced unrest and discord amongst the Serbian people. Throughout their history, the Serbian people had never been as broken up as they are today. However, the Serbian people in all Serbian states and lands are waking up. We, the Serbian Chetniks, have put out the old flags of glory. We are the Serbian Chetniks are fighting - turn to the next page, please - for the restoration of a free and independent Serbian state in the Balkans. We will never be satisfied with Serbia as it now stands, as it now exists, narrowed down, almost reduced to the Belgrade district pashalic [phoen]. We, the Serbian Chetniks, only recognise the kind of Serbia which will comprise Serbian Macedonia, Serbian Montenegro Serbian Bosnia, Serbian Herzegovina, Serbian Dubrovnik, Serbian Dalmatia, Serbian Lika, Serbian Banija, Serbian Kordun, Serbian Slavonia, and Serbian Baranja." Did I say that at the rally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "We, the Serbian Chetniks, will not stop" -- you have the translation of the text in English. I'm being cautioned by the interpreters to slow down but, well, all right. Yes, for the French booth so I will slow down. "We, the Serbian Chetniks, will not stop until we realise this main goal of ours. We, the Serbian Chetniks, on all sides and in all Serbian states and lands, develop our political activities. "A while ago we saw this mob outside, this crowd outside that came to prevent us from what we intend to do." And what is in brackets is the response from the crowd so I'm not going to read it. "We, the Serbian Chetniks and Serbian people as a whole, the Orthodox Serbs, stretch out our hands towards our brothers, the Serbs of the Muslim faith." Do you remember me saying something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. "Throughout the course of Serbian history, there have always been great men of Muslim faith amongst our Serbian people. Let us just remember Mesa Selimovic, one of our greatest writers. We will never forget that the vice-president of the National Committee of Draza Mihajlovic was the heroic Mustafa Mulalic. We will never forget that one of the Chetnik military leaders, Vojvodas belonging to Draza Mihajlovic was Ismet Pupovac, a hero who commanded 2.000 Serbs of Muslim faith. However, we will also never forget this unruly crowd. It was people like these who killed Serbs throughout Bosnia, Herzegovina, both before and during the First World War and in this restricted and narrowed down Serbia of today. "We will never forget that such an unruly crowd in 1941 was the first to put on Ustasha uniforms and set off to slaughter the Serbs. "We will also never forget that throughout the course of Serbian history such an unruly crowd was always ready to serve all Serbian enemies to the very end, both the Austrians and the Germans, and everybody who attacked Serbia. We will never negotiate with an unruly crowd like that." Do you remember me saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You always delivered the same speech, almost word for word, at all your meetings and rallies, and the people you mentioned, Ismet Pupovac and Mustafa Mulalic and the figure of 2.000 or 3.000 Serbs, you would always list those things at each of your meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, this was a specific meeting geared towards a specific text because Muslims lived there. Where there were no Muslims I didn't say things like that, so I didn't repeat the same things everywhere. It was the same policy, the politics was the same and coincided in many points but not the same and not identical everywhere. Let me continue. "We, the Serbian Chetniks, are fighting for a Serbian state which will be democratic and freedom loving. A state of citizens completely equal to each other, with religious tolerance. We will, however, by no means allow throughout the Serbian lands the Islamic fundamentalists to roam and to dream about setting up a Pan-Islam Islamist state which would spread across the Balkans. They will see once again how heroic the Serbian people are and how steadfast they are in their intent" -- I haven't finished yet, don't move the text. "In their intent to restore the Serbian state, freedom, democracy," and now the next page or next column, "and their old glory. "We, the Serbian Chetniks, having waved our Serbian Chetnik flag and banner this year in our freedom-loving capital of Belgrade, place ourselves at the service of the Serb people and we will not give up on that. The Serbian Chetnik Movement is a party that enlists only the bravest, the most resolute and the most loyal to the Serbian people. The Serbian Chetnik Movement was formed as a party as early on as January of this year when the Serbian Freedom Movement was formed," and now we can skip that portion unless the Trial Chamber insists that we read everything because I'm referring to how this was established, so we can move on. Now I introduce my associates, Srdjan Glamocanin, Olivera Jelkic, Aleksandar Stefanovic, and so on and provide data about them.
