And then I go on to say all these associates that I've just mentioned, you can move the text down: "They were never afraid of police truncheons, they were never afraid of cordons and bans enforced by the regime, and it is with people like these, resolute, brave, and clever, that we managed to win legitimacy for our party. The communists banned at the beginning or from the beginning. Recently they wanted to stop us from holding a commemorative ceremony to mark the anniversary of General Draza Mihajlovic's death. They did not manage to do that because we brought out 10.000 people in front of the Prince Mihailo Obrenovic's monument in the centre of Belgrade." Do you remember the 17th of June, 1990, when we held a commemorative meeting for Draza Mihajlovic in Belgrade. All the papers wrote about that. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that the police banned the meeting but when they saw how many of us they were, they did not want to ban us. That's how it was. Now I go on to say the following. May we have the next paragraph, please. Our party was officially registered on a Tuesday, that's when the Serbian Chetnik Movement was officially registered. However, after this rally, we received a note saying that we were banned. Do you remember that the regime, in August 1990, refused to register the Serbian Chetnik Movement in Belgrade? All the papers wrote about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the papers did write about that but I am not sure I know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, I go on to talk about the party programme, we can move through that a little faster, we can skip some methods, but we say we fulfill all conditions and we just use peaceful methods of political struggle, and we act in conformity with the interests and aims of the Serbian people. And that is at the beginning of the third column, second paragraph. As such, the Serbian Chetnik Movement is at the service of its people. I spoke from my head then, I didn't have any paper in front of me, right? My speech was recorded and then a journalist of Velika Serbia published it, put it down on paper and even put where the applause took part -- took place. The Serbian Chetnik Movement is in favour of a -- the restoration of a democratic political system, a multi-party system, the setting up of the rule of law which means legitimate authorities and the legality of their decisions. It is for an independent court and public attorney system and preventing any political party from recruiting the army and police into its ranks. You will remember that under the Communist regime, every policeman and every officer and lower ranking officer had to be a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia; that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, do you remember that? It's important.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not important as far as I am concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that how it was, though?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ask me something else, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have a lot of time, an abundance of time. I have more than an hour so I can go through all these things. And the time that the Judges used up and the Prosecutor is deducted from my time so I have a lot of time. The Serbian Chetnik Movement supports abandoning the policy of non-alignment and then I go on to condemn cooperation and alliances with states led by Idi Amin, Bokassa and so on. And then I made a mistake, because I'm a little more mature now and [indiscernible] I say, We the Serb Chetniks promote the return of our fatherland to Europe to a community of civilised and democratic nations and states. Later on we came to realise that there were the fewest civilised states precisely in Europe, so we don't want that anymore. So that's the correction I would like to make after gaining a better understanding and developing my consciousness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we are not going read out this entire speech; it's pages long.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll skip over some sections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you remember whether a Muslim took the floor during this meeting; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because Mr. Seselj, at the very end, there is a person taking the floor called Sakib Kavazovic saying, "I am a Muslim." It might be interesting to see what this person has to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, let us first find if this sentence that is being quoted in the indictment can be found in this speech. This is what I was thinking of. If you permit me, I have time and I was planning. Look, if the sentence is not in my speech then that whole part of the indictment can be dropped. I don't have any further reason to examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This sentence is not in the document that we have in our hands. That's very obvious.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So do you want me to just discard everything that I was intending to read?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this sentence was actually said on August 4th, no, it's not in the speech that you delivered on August 4th, that's absolutely sure. We don't need to read the entire thing just to conclude the sentence is not included.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. When I finished this speech then the citizens present began to ask questions; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the first question was put by a person who did not introduce himself. He asked something about Tito's mausoleum in Dedinje, and this is on the page before last and then I answered his question. And then the next person is Ratko Cvetkovic who introduced himself as the Serbian National Renewal member from Milici. This is a different municipality next to Bratunac, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He asked a question so I answered him. Then another person who did not give his name said that he would have complications at work because of attending our meeting. And then the fourth question, a citizen asks about the position of the peasants and what is our position on that. And then again the fifth question is by a person who begins putting the question with the words, "Comrades," and at the end when we wanted to finish there was someone coming towards the lectern. And now look, a person broke through, this is the 36th page, he began to speak but the frenetic applause made it impossible to hear him, Vojvoda, look, well, it is obvious that I am the only Vojvoda present. So then he says, God be with you. Actually, I say first, "Brothers, please wait for this gentleman to say what he wants to say and then we will go outside together to see who is threatening us." And then the crowd replied, "Hear, hear," and then this person came up to the lectern and he said, "God be with us Serbian brothers and sisters." And the crowd replied, "God be with you." Then he said, "I am a Muslim, Sakib Kavazovic from Semberija. In 1951 I was forced to cross over to Serbia and I have lived in Serbia since 1951. I built one house there but I couldn't say. I went amongst Serbian brothers. Now I lived in Novo Selo in Macva for five years, four years in Lesnica. I have lived here for 25 years now and I am not afraid of anyone. I have my children here, my son got married in Valjevo, I live with Valjevo people, I fight for Serbia and I will die for Serbia." Then the journalist comments, "Everybody rises fervently greeting brother Muslim with applause. The Vojvoda goes up to him and kisses him. The crowd greets this gesture with even more fervour." The president of the Mali Zvornik local board of the Serbian Chetnik Movement, addresses the crowd again, If there are no further questions, I would like to ask us all to go out with dignity and without provocations, no provocations from our side, but then when we went out, we were hit by stones. That's how it was. Do you remember the Muslim who came out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seselj, I left before this happened because I was taken out by your security. I wanted to say something, some people reacted but you said, Let him say what he wants to say, then these two people took me by the arms and without an incident, without harming me, they took me outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't speak at this meeting in any case, why would anyone throw you out no matter what you said at my meeting. I was able to hold rallies before large groups of people where more than 90 per cent of the people were against me and my sympathisers, but I still could deal with them. So whatever you wanted to say at this meeting, no one would have taken you out of the hall. This is just pure fabrication. You were not removed from the meeting, only somebody who was provoking violence or was violent would have been taken out of the meeting. So, since now we have finished this, are you still claiming that this meeting in Mali Zvornik was held in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did have that meeting in March 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Then by next week the Prosecutor will assemble all the articles from the newspapers and then we can see it here. As you know I have no associates and I have nobody who would be able to help me to search for these things myself. All that I have here in front of me is the things that I have received from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, before the break, the Trial Chamber has one question. Is there an audiotape of the speech you delivered on August 4th, 1990? Is there an audiotape? An audio recording of this speech? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something that you would need to ask journalist Vineta Marinovic, I have no contacts with her. If the Prosecution is able to find her but this is not very likely. This took place more than -- or almost 20 years ago, so I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you identified quite justly that this part of the indictment was very crucial and you wondered whether someone really heard what was said. You knew that a newspaper article had been drawn up from it. Fine. Now, the news reporter who transcribed your speech might have done so from an audiotape recording that she would have had. If that's the case, one of your associates, and you have many, could have went to see this reporter, ask her for the audiotape and that would be an evidence for you, you know, to say that, Listen to this speech, you can listen to the entire speech and I never said this sentence. But didn't think about this, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as -- in the same way that somebody, when they publish an article can drop something, omit saying something, they can also delete something from a tape. I mean it never occurred to me that that would be something important. What is important here is actually when the meeting was held, the date, and then only after what was actually said at the meeting. I could have said the worst things in the world at a meeting in 1990. This is two years before the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj. But you'll reckon with me, if this audiotape does exist, maybe the news reporter kept it or maybe it's in the archives of the newspaper. It could be very useful for you as evidence for your case. Furthermore, Mr. Seselj, you have many associates, and these associates should have scrutinised all the newspapers, all issues of this newspaper at the time to prove that nothing had happened in March 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my collected works already number about 104 or 105 volumes of 1.000 pages each and almost all my text about myself and about the Serbian Party and about the Serbian Chetnik Movement are published in those tomes. The Hague Prosecution has an earlier edition of those works. They have some 80 volumes. So every speech from the Radical Party is in that collection especially from volumes 41 to 50. Everything that was ever written about the Radical party would be in that, so if there had been a meeting in Mali Zvornik it would be contained there. You're behaving as if I had the burden of proof. Actually this burden is on the Prosecution, the very fact that the meeting did not take place in March 1992 but in August 1990 is enough to overturn the whole indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Mr. Seselj, you're right. The burden of proof is on the Prosecution, everyone knows that. But you are the accused in this case and you have to defend yourself so you should say, I'm being accused of something because it was something I said in a speech, I would have said in a speech allegedly, I'm going to prove and demonstrate that this is not the right speech and that in the speech I actually gave I never said this. If you have an audiotape, an audio recording that could back this, this would be crucial evidence for you. You're saying my speech is in my book. Fine. But your speech could have been redacted, you know, you could have cut off some sensitive excerpts whereas in an audiotape we have the reality of things. We can know technically whether the audiotape has been tampered with or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is Velika Serbia issue number 3 magazine of the 15th of August, 1990, when no one in the Balkans knew that war was imminent. This is August 1990. The least they knew was that at some point, there would be The Hague International Tribunal for War Crimes which would be established and where I would be expected to defend myself against war crimes, the illegal Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, don't make things worse. You're talking -- you're saying -- just said "illegal Tribunal." You could have spared that. You could have not said this and proof of -- we're really trying to do our job as Judges here, full independence. But now we'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-2000, do you consider me to be an uneducated person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, why?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you believe that I lack some elementary theological knowledge pertaining to modern religions that I have no idea what that is about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't wish to discuss that with you, but at no point did I say that you were an uneducated man. Actually, as a matter of fact, and you heard me well, I said yesterday that you were the youngest lawyer with a Ph.D. in Yugoslavia and you must have and had to have learned something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In my indictment, it says that I had called Bosnian Muslims pagans and in the pre-trial brief that I had called them Godless. Would any educated person refer to Muslims as Godless at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: For example, if I know that Mohammed created a new religion based on Christian and Judaic heritage and that he adopted their beliefs and formed them, gave them a new form but kept the faith in the one and only God, how can I then refer to them as Godless? You know that Muslims recognise Christ as a prophet, you know that, you're a Muslim, aren't you? How do Muslims call Jesus Christ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Isa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Isa Messiah or Isa the prophet and you know that in the Koran, when the day of judgement comes, it says that Isa Meremi [phoen], Jesus of Mary will judge the living and the dead. Is this mentioned in the Koran?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Muslims only do not recognise Jesus as the son of God but they do recognise him as a God's prophet, Islam recognises that. And do you know that in Syria, there is a mosque dedicated to Jesus Christ, Ici Pedombet [phoen]. It's a mosque that is God knows how old that is dedicated to Jesus. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well I'm not that informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, but I am. What I'm trying to let you know is that it is quite impossible for me to use this term and as much as my speeches are quite radical and forceful, sometimes even extreme, still I do not commit such stupidities in my speeches. My speeches are logical and coherent, aren't they? Do you disagree with that logic? You cannot say that my speeches have no internal logic and coherence, would you agree with that? You're quiet? Did you study law in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know what to answer other than yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you can say yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well this is your theory. I do not want to get involved in your theories and your views. I don't want to take any part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Let's move to a new question and let's hope it's something that is a much calmer atmosphere. Would a more calm atmosphere suit you or a more turbulent one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A more turbulent one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well I'm going to proceed calmly. You gave two statements to The Hague Prosecution; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You gave a statement in 1996 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber would rather have a very smooth and quiet hearing. You haven't understood. Well you're asking the witness whether he'd rather have a quiet hearing. I associate myself with you and I can tell you that the Trial Chamber also would rather have a very quiet hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. On my part, I'm going to do my best but you saw what happened earlier. I had a concept of cross-examination. The Prosecutor wanted to break that up right at the beginning, disrupt that so I couldn't deal with it in the way that I wished. The Prosecutor got stuck to this point what year and so on so I have to go down another track. I mean the over ambition of the Prosecutor spoiled things this time but now we are going to improve things. We will make them better.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You gave your first statement in 1996; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then you provided a statement in 2002; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The first statement you referred to the things that were asked of you yesterday during the examination in chief and the second statement was part of the preparation by the Prosecution for the Naser Oric trial but then they never called you to testify; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see that they asked you here about some things about your war experiences or work together with Naser Oric and events from 1993 but we're not going to go into that. The second statement has nothing to do with this case; isn't that right? Do you remember your second statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it but we didn't discuss the Oric trial at all. What was discussed was for me to state my story and to say what I knew that would make some sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you talked about some other things, they probably didn't tell you why they were seeking your statement but judging by the contents of that statement, I see that they insisted on that because there are names here of various Muslim leaders, military leaders and so on, but we're not going to go into that. This is not so important now. In this first statement, you first talk about how you set up a checkpoint at the stone quarry and arrested four Serb police officers and seized their car; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What date was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 8th of April, in the morning, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the morning. So this was before this armed clash in Zvornik which occurred during the day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during the day or a little bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: During the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the attack on Zvornik, the proper attack on Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was your authority to stop a police vehicle, first of all? Secondly, to arrest four policemen, and then to confiscate their car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know very well Mr. Seselj that before the beginning of the war, checkpoints were set up everywhere where the Serb and the Muslim populations lived close by, so these were set up to separate them. So wherever it suited anyone, they would set up a checkpoint and they would monitor who was moving along that particular road, what did they have in the car, what was their business.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So in Vlasenica, there were no combat actions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the situation was the same as Zvornik. There was some preparations but nothing was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. So these were policemen from Vlasenica, they wore the same uniforms as any police officers in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in civilian clothing. Only one of them had camouflage uniform with a red polo neck top.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It doesn't say that here, only that they were police officers and that you confiscated their car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw that they were police officers on the basis of their IDs. Three of them were wearing civilian clothing and one --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You as a group of citizens with weapons stopped a police car and arrested four policemen. They showed you their IDs and you looked at them and on the basis of their documents, you could see that they were ethnic Serbs. They were not Serb police officers. There was no Serb police in Vlasenica, the police were still one united force at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. Throughout the whole territory of eastern Bosnia, the police had separated already, so the police in Vlasenica were separated just as it was in Mali Zvornik so the Vlasenica police had its own -- Serb police had its own direction and why we stopped them was because they had weapons, they had explosives and they also had casks in their car.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then when you stopped them, you called the Zvornik police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And a Muslim policeman from Zvornik told you to release them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he checked the names of the people that we dictated to them and he said that they should be returned to -- towards Vlasenica through the checkpoints of Konjevic Polje which was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How did you return them if you seized their vehicle, you didn't give them the car back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of those people who was driving gave it back. They drove them in that car to the Serb checkpoint in Vlasenica and seized the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They seized the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On what grounds? On the grounds of the rules of war; is that right? All right. Very well. So now you're taking this car and you went to Zvornik to the police station and then you say, On the first floor of the police station building, I saw three men who were tied or attached one to another with handcuffs, they were handcuffed one to another. How many of them were, three or four?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were four.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that fourth one you didn't see?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer, the speakers are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now let's deal again with those four people who were arrested, who were arrested at the checkpoint at the entrance to Zvornik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the northern side and there's a river there called Zlatica [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You say one of them wore a camouflage uniform and the other two were in civilian clothes; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I referred to the uniforms, they were policemen. The others all wore uniforms, all four of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see. Because on page 5 of your statement here, the last paragraph, you describe them, those thee men and this is what you say, One of them had a camouflage uniform and the other two were in civilian clothes. That's what it says in this statement. Were they all wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what I said in my statement but anyway, one was in a pattern camouflage uniform, the others were in regular, ordinary uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Here it says civilian clothes and that shows the lack of seriousness on the part of the OTP. "The fourth colleague, Repic, I saw in Fadil Mujic's office."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he was chief of -- a chief in the Zvornik police and he works in the MUP of Tuzla today. And you say: "I saw a heap of scrap wire, the kind of wire you use for suffocating people. Wires and injection and some other objects with you the police uncovered during the interrogation. I saw the wires in the hall outside the room in which the three men were held."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 72 pieces of wire. The people counted them, and on the table there were 72 pieces of wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what did Fadil Mujic say to you when you saw these people? Who are they? Did he say anything about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was conducting his interrogation, his questioning, and I told him, I said Fadil, the shooting had already started from the northern part of the municipality from the nearby hill, from where the Chetniks started to take over the territory, this shooting, the war has started officially and you're sitting here questioning people. Now if you consider that they should be released then release them. Let's not make any more -- any incident about this. Let's try and calm the situation again and that's what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So your idea was to have the people released. That was your first idea?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And were they beaten during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody touched them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't see any traces of blows on their body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I talked to one of them, I was at a distance of say two metres, and I just asked him some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know the names of those people today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just know that the man that Fadil was examining had the nickname Repic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that it's Dusko Vuckovic, nicknamed Repic one of the greatest criminals in the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that he was taken to trial in Serbia for crimes committed in the Zvornik area and that he committed suicide in prison, you don't know any of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right let's see what you go on to say here: "When I saw Repic for the first time, he was sitting on a chair with his back to me. He had broad shoulders, a broad neck." This is on page 6, second paragraph, and he had his hair in a ponytail. The lower half the his neck was shaved. He might have been 25 or 26 years old at the time and although he was sitting down I think he was probably tall, about 1 metre 80. He had light brown hair and when he turned towards me, I saw that he had side burns. His face was red, and he didn't have a beard or mustaches. He had bald patches above his ears. He turned to me and he asked Fadil, what did they tell me to release the policemen from Vlasenica, and Fadil said that the chief of police Osman Mustafic, who lives in Germany today, knew the four men and that's why he told me to release them. And that refers to the Serb policemen from Vlasenica whom you released; right? And this is your description of Repic, and it corresponds to a great measure to what the man actually looks like. It's a reliable description of Dusko Vuckovic, aka Repic so you have a very good memory if I can note that. Now, there's another paragraph, and I'll quote that. You say: "I went back into the room in which the three men were kept. I sat next to one of them who was thin and I turned to him and said, 'You scum, who sent you here and what are you doing here?' And he introduced himself. I don't remember what his name was," that's your comment. And he said that he was from Pancevo and that the media, it was the media's fault that he was there because he said that he spent a month and a half with many others in quarantine because they kept saying that the Muslims in Zvornik are slaughtering and putting Serbs on the spit and rubbing salt into their wounds. He didn't say where he was in quarantine with these other Serbs." So that is your statement. Now on that occasion, did you have any information as to how these people identified who they were, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any information on paper but people told me, the people that I found in the corridor outside, they said that they were Chetniks and that wires were found on them and so on, and all the other objects, but I didn't ask for any identifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that some documents were found on them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some documents were found but I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you don't know what documents ID cards or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now I'm going to tell you who these people were. Milorad Ulemek, nicknamed Legija was one; Vojin Vuckovic, nicknamed Zuca was another; Dusko Vuckovic -- or Dusan Vuckovic, nicknamed Repic was another; and then there was Miroslav Bogdanovic. Do you know today who those people are?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Vojin Vuckovic later on, after the fall of Kula Grad, within the Territorial Defence he set up a detachment called Igor Markovic and afterwards, that detachment came to be known of the Yellow Wasps. Have you heard of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: His brother Repic was well known for some atrocious crimes that were committed there and for which he was tried. Milorad Ulemek, Legija, he later became one of Arkan's men and then transferred to the police of Serbia. He was the commander of a unit there, a special police unit and had the rank of colonel, and then he was arrested and taken to trial because of his alleged involvement in the killing Prime Minister Zoran Djindjic. Did you ever link those things up on the basis of what the papers wrote and so on? Did you ever bring them into contact with their roles later on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I read various articles about some of them, the ones you mention and the dirty things they were involved in, but I didn't enter into any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Miroslav Bogdanovic died in 1993. Now, my associates in June last year visited Milorad Lukovic aka Legija in the central prison in Belgrade, took a statement from him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could I ask the usher to provide a copy of the statement to the Trial Chamber and the Prosecutor and place one on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's a statement written over five pages by hand, it's in handwritten form, so let's read it through together and see what it says because Milorad Ulemek, Legija, for a time had the surname of Lukovic. He explains how he came to be Zvornik, so let's see how he describes those events, the events that you refer to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it up on our screens, the screen that the public can see, because this is a public matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, this was sent to me on the 23rd of January this year from Belgrade; it was faxed to me, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, you will notice that yesterday, in direct examination, I led no evidence on this point whatsoever. I don't know why the accused is now going to read out a long statement from someone who had given no evidence about this and it is irrelevant to the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the cross-examination is not the right you have to ask any question. You should base your questions on those questions that have been put during examination-in-chief. Which topic are you addressing now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness testified about the war events in Zvornik as he experienced them, and from his statement I can see that he met these four men and even talked to them. Secondly, some other witnesses earlier on referred to these people as well. We discussed them. There was a witness who claimed that two of them had membership cards of the Serbian Radical Party, if you recall. I'd like to remind you of those witnesses. I didn't have Milorad Lukovic's statement at the time, we had Vojin Vuckovic, Zuco's statement. Vojin Vuckovic, Zuco, is the one I quoted, so let's deal with this matter because it's important for me. What the witness testified about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to specify that the fact that topics are being discussed during cross-examination which were not addressed during examination-in-chief, this is not a problem as far as I'm concerned because cross-examination deals with the defence of the accused; but as far as this particular statement is concerned, I would like to emit reservations and I have already done this on a number of times. Every time the accused shows us statements like this one, I don't need to repeat those reservations I have already made, I would just like to say that I don't agree with such statements that have no probative value, not even prima facie, so I cannot accept these. This is my personal view, as you know, Mr. Seselj. I have repeated this many a time. I just need to repeat it again today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Lattanzi, I'm not offering up any statements into evidence here; I'm just using these statements as a ground work for the cross-examination. I want to ask the witness whether he has some of his own knowledge about what Milorad Ulemek aka Legija speaks about in his statement, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, but since I have said this several times before, as far as I am concerned, you may put these questions but you shouldn't read this statement and you shouldn't put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you say to the witness, right, we have this statement. In this statement, Mr. Legija says such and such and then you ask the witness what he thinks about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do you want me to continue or Mr. Marcussen?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Here, Milorad Ulemek - let's have it on the ELMO - and his nickname was Legija, provides data about himself, when he was born, who his parents were. The statement was certified by the prison authorities and it was signed as well, it's signed at the end. The statement was sent to me, to the detention unit fax machine, and it's not very legible because the detention unit usually makes a photocopy when a fax comes in for me and then provides me with the photocopy and put the original in my file. However, I think we will be able to make due with this, at least I hope so. In the first paragraph he says that he was in the foreign legion in Chad and when he saw what was going on in Yugoslavia, he escaped from the foreign legion and in 1992, arrived in Yugoslavia to help his own people out. And he says that he decided to go to Bosnia to help the Serbs there and protect them, as far as he could, for them to defend themselves against the Muslim terrorists. Now, witness, do you know whether these four men, during the interrogation, which went on for a long time because they were arrested on the 7th at the barricade and spent the whole night in the police station and only the next day towards evening were released; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 8th in the morning at 4.30 a.m., and the distance is one kilometre and they were in the police station within 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they say where they went and why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, talking to the people who took them in and questioned them, I learned that they wanted to infiltrate the town and be a point of support for other people coming in from the hills to reconnoitre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that what they said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was told they had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, here Legija says that he wanted to join the Vuk Draskovic Guard, first of all, commanded by the late Giska but that he changed his mind because Vuk was unreliable and you couldn't count on him. And then he goes on to say that before he went to the foreign legion he knew Nedjo Boskovic. Do you know who Nedjo Boskovic was at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard that but I don't know that, I don't know that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure you don't know him but he was the chief of the military security service in the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he was head of the security service in the Yugoslav Army for a few months, so that's the position he occupied, and he said that he knew him before he went to join the foreign legion because he was the father of a friend of his from primary school, a little girl. And he says that when he returned in 1992 to the homeland, Nedjo Boskovic came into contact with me straight away, he says. Now while these four men were at the police station in Zvornik, did Nedjo Boskovic call up from Belgrade to ask about them? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know. Very well, because we had testimony about that from a witness. Did you know who Milan Petrovic, Zuda [phoen], was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's from your parts. Now Pusula, that nickname, I knew somebody from his family who was a hauler but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was a hauler himself, and do you know that he was well known for black marketeering in weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one of them was a black marketeer so it must have been that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's him. So you knew that he was a black marketeer in weapons, dealt in weapons. Now here is what Legija says. He says that Nedjo Boskovic, at the beginning of April, told him that a certain Milan Petrovic, nicknamed Pusula, was bringing weapons in clandestinely to Zvornik and that he ought to be arrested, and that he took on this assignment as a patriotic act because he found it intolerable that a Serb should supply Muslims with weapons clandestinely, because they used those weapons to kill Serbs. So he said that was the assignment given him by the chief of the military security service whom he knew earlier on, General Nedjo Boskovic to go to Zvornik and in the Zvornik area, to arrest Milan Petrovic, nickname Pusula?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did he have an address this Pusula man?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, he doesn't say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pusula didn't live in the town of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was in the Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but not in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He later on says that they lost their way. You didn't know that they were criminals at the time and they weren't criminals at the time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's something you're telling me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When I say that this man Repic was a criminal later on, that Vojin Vuckovic formed the Yellow Wasps, that Miroslav Bogdanovic died in that of 1993 and wasn't involved in any criminal affairs, and that Legija was first of all in Arkan's unit and then he transferred to work in the police station and reach the rank of Colonel, that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, if you permit me. I will say that in your speeches, and I've been following that, you keep saying that some members of some other parties, some other units, the Wasps, the Wolves, that they all were in the Chetniks in the area of the Zvornik municipality. The fact that later they found pretty names, attractive names like Eagles, Wasps and Eagles, actually, basically they were all Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All the Serbian fighters actually were Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... has no value but this Legija seemingly wrote this document whilst he was in prison. We can see that it says something in Italian on the letterhead of the paper, [Italian spoken], 23rd of January, 2009, 11 hours 10. Can you explain to us how you received this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this document was received by the detention unit at their fax, and this is the marking that -- or the stamp that that fax machine makes recently. I don't know what this means [Italian spoken], or whatever it says but it arrived at the detention unit on the 23rd of January, 2009 at 1110 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right all the faxes you receive read [Italian spoken] that's on the letterhead. Continue please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He says here that he went to Zvornik with Miroslav Bogdanovic, with the two Vuckovic brothers, Zuco and Repic; and that the two of them, the Vuckovics, he saw them then for the first time, probably he knew Miroslav Bogdanovic from earlier, and he doesn't say that. In the night, between the 7th and the 8th of April 1992, we lost our way after crossing the bridge at the entrance to Zvornik. He says he didn't know that area and then instead of going to the right, they turned and went to the left, and they came up against an ambush of armed Muslims who captured us and take us -- took us to the SUP premises. Is it true that Muslims had set up barricades around Zvornik, and that there were armed Muslims at those barricades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had crossed the bridge, could not have gone -- they could only have gone to the left, if we're talking about these two bridges, there are only two bridges, there's one in Karakaj. They didn't cross that bridge. If they had taken the city bridge, then they could have gone to the right, and they were found, concealed in a ditch that goes through there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They passed by the Serbian barricade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the Muslim barricade at the entrance of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If they had crossed at Karakaj they would have crossed to the -- turned to left and went directly to the town. Had they turned to the right they would have encountered the Serb barricade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They couldn't have gone to the right. It was the Karakaj industrial facility, and there were no Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Serbs were there. So instead of turning to the right, they turned to the left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would they turn right if Zvornik is to the left?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are overlapping, the interpreter can no longer certify the accuracy of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please wait a few minutes before you answer. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Look, they are going to do some confidential assignment for the JNA military security service, and they probably got instructions that after they crossed the Karakaj bridge if they turned left they would encounter Serbian police. Instead of turning to the right, they turned to the left, and they encountered a Muslim barricade. This is logical to me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not logical to me, Mr. Seselj, that precisely on the day of the attack on Zvornik, they set off to carry out some assignment. Why didn't they do it some days before if that is what they wanted to do, and if the person that you are talking about happened to be in town on that day, he could have been in town only before the attack on Zvornik took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you think that the conflict was planned on the 8th of April. It could have broken out on the 9th or the 11th. It was evident that the conflict would occur, but it wasn't planned to take place on that day; is that correct? Maybe this capture of theirs speeded up the conflict. Did you release them afterwards? Somebody threatened, you released them, or we will attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such threats because nobody knew that they had entered town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. But Nedjo Boskovic called by phone to ask about them, and he sent a TV crew even requesting to speak to them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was there a Serbian television crew arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well let's see what he says after that. He said that they were taken to the SUP premises and then while they were being arrested, they took our particulars and then he said these three immediately showed their membership cards of Arkan's Serbian volunteer guards, and I had my military ID with me which I presented to a Muslim senior officer; and I told them I was on a special assignment. That's what he told him. Did you find a military ID card on him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if we found a military ID card on him. What I'm saying is that I went had inside and I was in there perhaps for three minutes at the most, while I told Fadil Mujic what I told him, that he need today release these people so that we would avoid war and the worst from occurring; and perhaps I asked in some 60 seconds one of those three members what I asked them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. And then Legija said immediately they began to beat us, and they handcuffed us, especially diligent in this was a police officer who was addressed as Asim, as far as I can recall. This Asim beat us the most and soon -- with whatever he could lay his hands on. At one point, he tried to cut my ear off and precisely when he wanted to do that, as he was holding my ear in one hand, and a knife in the other, a senior officer entered the room where all of this was happening and then stopped him from carrying this out. Do you know about any policeman called Asim who happened to be there at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know a man by the name of Asim, and it's true that he was one of the senior figures in the police, but he wasn't there when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is his last name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. After two hours of a group beating, we were locked up in separate rooms. I was all bloody from the beating and later I saw that the others were in the same state. This officer who saved me from getting my ear cut off whispered at one point that he was going to try to help us. In the end, it turned out that this was Fadil Mujic, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that he left Zvornik with Serb aid on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. It's not true. I have completely opposite information, which is 100 percent accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Legija said that in the morning, members of the green berets arrived at the SUP, and I heard that they were asking these local policemen to hand us over to them so they could take us to Kula Grad and that's where they would execute us, this is what he heard. When these members of the Green Berets were talking to the policemen, were there any green berets there present in the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about such a formation of the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You never heard of the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard with them, but there was no such formation among the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear about the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How long had it existed in the Muslim area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the late 1991, perhaps just before the new year when the conflicts broke out in Croatia and when these attempts at separation or division of municipalities occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware the Green Berets are a military formation of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just heard about it, but I never saw these units and they didn't have any documents or were never registered as Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We will talk about that later. I have some material, so it will be interesting to discuss that later. Legija said that while their senior officers were talking amongst themselves the others began to beat us again. This lasted for a half an hour or so and I fainted from the beating. When I came to, I found out that a TV crew from Serbia had stopped by. Do you know that a TV crew from Serbia appeared before the police station Mali Zvornik. This was in the morning on the 8th of April before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflict began early in the morning by very strong shelling of the whole of Zvornik especially the part where perhaps some resistance was being expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was the artillery being fired in the direction of Kula Grad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was being fired from the entrance to Zvornik towards the direction of Karakaj, so Zvornik was attacked already in the morning. I don't know about this TV crew, but I imagine that they could not have entered because the war had already began by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But we had witnesses who mentioned this. Then he said, I knew that they were sent by Nedjo Boskovic so that he would protect us and he saw this footage later on television when he was released, perhaps on Belgrade or Novi Sad television and since he had talked with Fadil Mujic he knew what was happening to us. So Legija claims that Nedjo Boskovic had spoken by telephone with Fadil Mujic; do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When was this time because when these people were questioned, was it then? When they were questioned? When they were beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't really speak to Fadil about anything at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Legija said that he was told that the attack on Zvornik began around noon and that the number of policemen and members of the Green Berets in the SUP building went down considerably, that he heard firing, not far from the building. And then at one point he asked one of the guards guarding us to unlock his hand cuffs. I told him that I had unbearable pain, and that I couldn't stand it anymore since my hands were hand cuffed behind my back, and that he could put the hand cuffs back on but with my hands in front. He did that and he notes that those guards were guarding them were all of proper behaviour, and they didn't beat them or abuse them. At that point in time, there were four of us in the office. Not long after that, we were separated again. Zuco and his brother were taken to another office and the two of us stayed in one office at one point. There was an opportunity for me, and I managed to take a rifle from one of the guards. While I was disarming the other guard with a pointed rifle at him ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber is really wondering what the point to this is? We're wasting time. What is the point, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that in the last year you have seen that everything I do has some sense. We can see that Zuco and his brother arrived as a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party to Zvornik, and I am denying that I -- I deny that in 1992, he had anything to do with the Serbian Radical Party. I already presented evidence that he formed the Igor Markovic Detachment only after the 26th of April after Kula Grad fell. I mean, what do you mean, what does it serve? This is the purpose of it. This is why I'm doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put the question to him. He was at the police station. Saw the four of them. Put the question to him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this witness who has the tendency to exaggerate his wartime role said that it was his idea to free these or release these four people you heard that with his own ears. Well let's see what Legija says about them being released, how Fadil Mujic freed them and how then he made it possible for Mujic to leave and to go abroad through Serbia. Why are you preventing me from doing this? I don't have anything to talk about regarding the conflict in his village of birth and the neighbouring villages. This is not in my indictment. I didn't research that, and I have no idea what was going on there about a fight where -- or if there was a house where women were detained and sexually abused. I was nothing to do with that. I am trying to clarify things that are directly related to my indictment especially that I'm now all alone and that I have no associates anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you need to know whether these four were volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party. That's the essence of it. So just put the question to him directly. He'll say yes or no, these were Arkan's men, this or that. Put the question to him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this could be so in case the witness were neutral in relation to the proceedings, and if he wished to testify on facts; but you saw that the witness was hostile to me even during the examination in chief. I mean these direct questions mean nothing to me. I have to ask questions in a roundabout way to drag out of the witness what is relevant if that is possible. If it's not possible, then forget it. You gave me two hours, then allow me to use those two hours. I'm not an illiterate, uneducated person not to know what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So then he said that he disarmed two guards and then Fadil Mujic entered who was afraid when he saw him with a gun inside and then he said that Fadil Mujic told him then that he helped them that night when he came in and found one of the police officers trying to cut his ear off. This was something that Fadil Mujic prevented from happening and he said that they would help them to escape from Zvornik. Legija said he kept that promise around 1600 hours, he managed to get them out of the SUP building and to drive them towards the Zvornik barricade which was held by the JNA and that on the way, Mujic asked him that he should help him in turn by helping him to cross over into Serbia. This is something that Legija is saying.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say something now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Go ahead, I am stating this so you could give your comments.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it's not true and does not make sense that I am hostile towards you. Why would I? This is your case, and I am here a witness; and I would like to honourably and honestly state what I know. You are presenting some details to me here and already in my statement I said that I don't know any details, but I explained all the things that I saw when I entered the police administration and what -- I saw these four people who were arrested, I didn't know their names at the time. I told Fadil that he should release these people if he had no evidence, but I also suggested that he should get in touch with Asim Hadzic, who was at Kula Grad, and he was coordinating the defence efforts there. I told him to get in touch with him and later I spoke with Asim Hadzic, later, I spoke with him about it, and he said that he had called Fadil Mujic on the phone and asked him to release them. Fadil Mujic released those people, and they went out through the hydro-electric power plants close to the police administration. He didn't go to Serbia. He couldn't leave through Serbia. He passed through my village and went, taking a different direction via Snagovo. That's what that settlement is called, and then he went in the direction of Kalesija and Tuzla. This is the direction he took to leave. So it's not true that he left through Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, gentlemen, you can see that we found out something important, that Asim Hadzic intervened from Kula Grad with Fadil Mujic to release these four people. Kula Grad was a Muslim fortification near Zvornik. The Muslims were in a very good position there, and they were prepared for combat there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, this is a very good thing, it's a very good deed that this person did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, we're not giving our value judgements here, only the facts are important.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well this is an important fact that this man released these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, we see that there was another man there and told Fadil Mujic to have the people released. We didn't know that before. Nobody's yet said that. We saw earlier on that Fadil Mujic released these men, but we haven't heard so far that Asim was involved; and we didn't know about your role in all that either. So this is a very important question as far as I'm concerned. Now, Legija goes on to say that Asim told him or rather Fadil Mujic told him that his family was already in Serbia because he transferred them when the conflict was imminent in Zvornik and Legija says that his conduct was very proper, and he's referring to Fadil Mujic. He said I helped him, and when we arrived across to Serbia, I managed to find a car to have him drive to see his family. I never heard or saw him after that and I sincerely hope that he's alive and well and managed today meet up with his family. Now, I don't want to explain the reasons why this is important for me how Fadil Mujic went from Zvornik, left from Zvornik; so let's hear your version, but don't mention the name of the place you live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 100 percent correct. Fadil Mujic did pass through my village and he spent several nights there, he slept there for several nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What date was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about the date but after the people were released, he spent three or four nights in my village and I know personally, I know the man personally, and he knows me. We talked and then he left via Snagovo and a built-up area towards Kalesija and the free territory of Tuzla. So it is unfounded, an unfounded fact that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 100 per cent, that's 100 per cent correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to do, to clear that up and it's important to me for certain reasons of my own to explain how Fadil Mujic came to leave Zvornik. Now, Legija goes on to say that the four of them went to the Jezero Hotel in Mali Zvornik. You know where the hotel is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps some 300 metres downstream from the hydroelectric power plant that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that there was the JNA headquarters and Serbian Territorial Defence staff was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In Hotel Jezero. And he says they reported to the staff there to say that they were alive and well and he says despite the fact that he had been beaten up, he wanted to become part and parcel of the struggle, the fighting, and he explains his motives for fighting for the Serb people. And he says they told me at the Territorial Defence staff, at Jezero hotel that there were certain forces in the factory in Karakaj. Did you know what Serb forces were in Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't down there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you heard about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well of course but in that area from Karakaj further down, the area was impopulated by a Serb majority and they were all part of Chetnik -- the Chetnik formations. And of course in the factory they had their staff and headquarters or administration or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's clear one thing up. The Muslims called all Serb fighters in this war Chetniks, didn't they, and the Serb fighters usually referred to themselves as Chetniks. That's not contentious. You keep repeating they were all Chetniks. I have nothing against that, you understand me but let's just clear that up. Now, this is what he says: When I arrived in Karakaj, I noticed armed people in a factory there and I asked them who their commander was and I learned that there were members of Arkan's guards there and members of the Territorial Defence of Zvornik as well. Did you know that Arkan's men were in Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony I said that Arkan's men or the people's known as Seselj's men were all over Serbia facing Karakaj and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now you're taking all this together. They were volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party there and you refer to them as Seselj's men, but they joined the action across the bridge in Zvornik itself, whereas Arkan's men started out from the direction of Karakaj. They didn't leave at the same time. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, because you are better informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, I am better informed. There were at least 100 volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party there, and I have certain Muslim information here to the effect that they estimate that there were about 2.000 soldiers on the Serb side. How many would you say there were, what would you say the Serb forces were in the Zvornik area, how many soldiers, a total of how many? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really couldn't say. I couldn't give you a figure, but if we know that there were 34 per cent -- that 34 per cent of the population was Serb in the area and they were all involved in one way or another --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, don't do any guesswork if you don't know. I have a book here provided me by The Hague Tribunal and it's Mirsad Hamdzic's book. He wrote a book called, "Zvornik: From the elections to Dayton," and in that book he says that the Serb forces numbered about 2.000 soldiers at the time, including policemen. Everybody, the Territorial Defence, the JNA, the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, Arkan's men, the White Eagles and all the rest, and he enumerates them. And we'll say later on some the characteristic details from that book. I have marked them if we have time, but let's just finish with Legija's statements. So you're not contending that it is possible that Arkan's men were in Karakaj and the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were in the town itself and that they went across the bridge into action. You're not challenging, are you, although you don't know for sure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for sure where they were deployed. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, he goes on to say, I didn't know Arkan personally until then but I respected him as a patriot and fighter. Arkan arrived in Karakaj that night. When we got to know each other, I explained who I was and everything that had happened to us and said that I wanted to join the fighting, if possible as a member of his unit. So that night was when Arkan and Legija met for the first time. The next morning was the last time I saw Miki, and that was the nickname for Miroslav Bogdanovic, and Zuco and Repic, they're the Vuckovic brothers, I never saw them after that. They simply disappeared somewhere. And then Legija goes on to say, Later on I heard that Zuco formed a unit of his own which was active as a paramilitary formation. With the Serbian volunteer guard, I took part in the liberation of Zvornik and later on Kula Grad, after which the guard withdrew because at Kula Grad Major Zika was killed. He was a fighter and officer in the Guard whom Arkan respected highly and loved. I assume you've heard of the Yellow Wasps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know when they were formed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear before you heard of the Yellow Wasps that there was a Niko Markovic detachment attached to the Territorial Defence of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is the first time I have heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. That completes this statement of Legija's. He goes on to describe how he went with Arkan's men to Sarajevo and says that he agrees that this statement be used in the trial at The Hague Tribunal, and that he was ready to be a defence witness but not via videolink but that he wanted to come in personally and testify in open session. All right. That's that. Now, before we go on to looking at some interesting details from this book, let me ask you this: When you enumerated the political parties active in Zvornik you mentioned the SDA party, the party of Democratic Action that rallied Muslims and that was formed first; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now whether it was formed first, I don't think so but they were formed parallelly, the political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was formed a little before the Serbian Democratic party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe half an hour before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Oh, no, let's not say things like that. You mention the Serbian Democratic party, now did you mention the party of the former Communist that's changed its name, the League of Communists became the SDP party, the Party for Democratic Change?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They took part in the elections?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they had a certain number of deputies in the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or a few, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, we have a list of those deputies in this book but that's not important. And you said that at the time the Serbian Radical Party existed too. You are the first witness who said here that the Serbian Radical Party existed in Zvornik before the conflict. Where did you get that piece of information from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You formed the Serbian Radical Party far before and the fact is that you spoke about meetings, rallies, and the war in Zvornik started on the 8th of April, therefore the party existed throughout Yugoslavia a long time before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, no, it didn't. That's the problem. It didn't. The party was still being organised in Serbia and you know that we were the last serious party to be registered in Serbia. We held a founding assembly of the unification of the Serbian Chetnik movement and most of the radical party was held only on the 23rd of February, 1991, in Kragujevac. And that's when the party began to branch out to different parts of Serbia. We had three initiation boards in the -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sarajevo, Bijeljina and Banja Luka, we had nothing in Zvornik. And you can't name a single man from the Serbian Radical Party from Zvornik before the war. I guarantee that. I guarantee that you cannot name a single name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the deputies were from among the Serb people and they went for consultations, the deputies of the SDS and the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Serb Serbian Radical Party did not have a single deputy how could they have gone for consultations. It didn't even take part in the elections. It's not there. It didn't exist and I have a list of parties that took part in the election. We have a list of those parties here by name. Lists.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the Serbs, amongst themselves, did not agree. There were the SDS men, Seselj's men, and they quarrelled amongst themselves. People couldn't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, please, if they had -- didn't have a united stand, there was far greater division amongst the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called themselves Seselj's men and the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amongst themselves they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Serbian Radical Party didn't exist. It had no headquarters in Zvornik at all. It didn't take part in the elections and it didn't have any deputy, not a single one. The party was formed only later in 1993 or 1994 in Zvornik but the first deputies were in the municipal assembly of Zvornik after the Dayton Accords, and then the Serbian Radical Party was the ruling party in Zvornik. After the Dayton Accords, did you hear that Seselj's radicals were in charge in Zvornik and in control there, not only Zvornik but other municipalities too? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, up until 1992, the party did not exist. You say that the whole of Snagovo was in the hands of the Serbian Radical Party when we didn't have a single member at the time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-2000 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how they declared themselves as Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, listen here. If somebody declares themselves a Chetnik, it doesn't mean that they are Serb radicals. Not all Chetniks were Serb radicals, I would like them to be but they're not, they weren't.
